chapter_text:
CHAPTER 13 - WORK AND ENERGY

Introduction

In everyday language the word 'work' is used loosely. A student who reads for hours says she has done a lot of work; a person standing still and holding a heavy suitcase also feels he is working hard. In science, however, 'work' has a precise meaning. Work is said to be done only when a force acts on an object AND the object moves through some distance in the direction of (or against) that force. Closely tied to work is the idea of energy - the capacity to do work. This chapter develops both ideas quantitatively, introduces the different forms of energy, the law of conservation of energy, and the concept of power.

13.1 WORK IN SCIENCE

Work is done when a force produces motion. If a constant force F acts on a body and the body moves a displacement s in the direction of the force, the work done is
   W = F s
More generally, if the displacement makes an angle theta with the direction of the force, only the component of the force along the displacement does work:
   W = F s cos(theta)
Here F is the magnitude of the force, s is the magnitude of the displacement, and theta is the angle between the force and the displacement.

Conditions for work to be done: (1) a force must act on the object, and (2) the object must be displaced. If either the force is zero or the displacement is zero, no work is done. A coolie who holds a load on his head and stands still does NO work in the scientific sense (s = 0), even though he gets tired - tiredness is a physiological effect, not scientific work.

Positive, negative and zero work:
 - POSITIVE WORK is done when the force (or its component) is in the same direction as the displacement; theta = 0 gives cos(0) = 1, so W = F s. Example: pushing a box forward and it moves forward.
 - NEGATIVE WORK is done when the force acts opposite to the displacement; theta = 180 degrees gives cos(180) = -1, so W = -F s. Example: friction opposing the motion of a sliding box; gravity on a ball thrown upward.
 - ZERO WORK is done when the force is perpendicular to the displacement; theta = 90 degrees gives cos(90) = 0, so W = 0. Example: the centripetal force on a body in circular motion, or carrying a bag horizontally while the lifting force is vertical.

SI unit of work: The SI unit of work is the JOULE (symbol J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves an object through 1 metre in the direction of the force: 1 J = 1 N x 1 m = 1 N m. A larger unit is the kilojoule: 1 kJ = 1000 J. Work is a scalar quantity (it has magnitude but no direction).

Worked example: A force of 15 N moves a body 3 m in the direction of the force. Work done = F s = 15 x 3 = 45 J.
Worked example: A force of 20 N is applied at 60 degrees to the horizontal and the body moves 5 m horizontally. W = F s cos(theta) = 20 x 5 x cos(60) = 20 x 5 x 0.5 = 50 J.

13.2 ENERGY

Energy is defined as the capacity (or ability) to do work. A body that can do work is said to possess energy, and the amount of energy a body possesses is measured by the total work it can do. Because energy is measured by work, energy has the SAME UNIT as work - the joule (J). Energy is also a scalar quantity.

There are many FORMS of energy:
 - Mechanical energy (kinetic + potential)
 - Heat (thermal) energy
 - Light energy
 - Sound energy
 - Electrical energy
 - Chemical energy (stored in fuels, food, batteries)
 - Nuclear energy (stored in the nucleus of atoms)
Mechanical energy - the energy a body has by virtue of its motion or its position - is the focus of this chapter, and it comes in two kinds: kinetic energy and potential energy.

13.3 KINETIC ENERGY AND THE WORK-ENERGY THEOREM

The energy possessed by a body because of its MOTION is called KINETIC ENERGY (KE). A moving hammer drives a nail, flowing water turns a turbine, a moving cricket ball can break a window - all because of their kinetic energy. For a body of mass m moving with speed v,
   KE = (1/2) m v^2
Kinetic energy is always positive and is measured in joules.

Derivation / Work-energy theorem: Suppose a body of mass m, initially at rest, is acted on by a constant force F and accelerates uniformly to speed v over a displacement s. By Newton's second law F = m a. Using the equation of motion v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s with u = 0 gives a = v^2 / (2 s). The work done by the force is W = F s = m a s = m (v^2 / 2s) s = (1/2) m v^2. This work has been stored in the body as kinetic energy. So
   W = (1/2) m v^2 = KE gained
This is the WORK-ENERGY THEOREM: the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, W = KE_final - KE_initial.

Worked example: A 2 kg ball moves at 4 m/s. KE = (1/2)(2)(4^2) = (1/2)(2)(16) = 16 J.
Worked example: A car of mass 1000 kg speeds up from 5 m/s to 15 m/s. Change in KE = (1/2)(1000)(15^2 - 5^2) = 500 x (225 - 25) = 500 x 200 = 100000 J = 100 kJ. The engine does 100 kJ of work.

13.4 POTENTIAL ENERGY

The energy possessed by a body because of its POSITION or CONFIGURATION is called POTENTIAL ENERGY (PE). A stone held above the ground, water stored in a dam, a stretched bow or a compressed spring all possess potential energy. GRAVITATIONAL potential energy is the energy a body has due to its height above the ground. To raise a body of mass m to a height h, we must do work against gravity equal to the weight (m g) times the height h:
   PE = m g h
where g is the acceleration due to gravity (about 9.8 m/s^2, often taken as 10 m/s^2 in problems). This work is stored as gravitational potential energy and can be recovered when the body falls.

Worked example: A 5 kg object is lifted to a height of 4 m (g = 10 m/s^2). PE = m g h = 5 x 10 x 4 = 200 J.

13.5 TRANSFORMATION OF ENERGY

Energy can change from one form to another. This is called TRANSFORMATION (or conversion) of energy. Examples: in an electric bulb, electrical energy changes to light and heat; in a loudspeaker, electrical energy changes to sound; in a battery, chemical energy changes to electrical energy; in a hydroelectric plant, the potential energy of stored water becomes kinetic energy of falling water, then electrical energy; during photosynthesis, light energy is stored as chemical energy in plants. In every such change the total amount of energy stays the same.

13.6 LAW OF CONSERVATION OF ENERGY

The LAW OF CONSERVATION OF ENERGY states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

Free-fall example: Consider a body of mass m dropped from a height H. At the top it is at rest, so KE = 0 and PE = m g H; the total mechanical energy is m g H. As it falls, height decreases so PE decreases, while speed increases so KE increases. At any point during the fall, KE + PE = m g H = constant. Just before hitting the ground (h = 0), PE = 0 and all the energy has become kinetic: (1/2) m v^2 = m g H, which gives v = sqrt(2 g H). At the half-way point (h = H/2) the energy is shared equally: KE = PE = (1/2) m g H. Thus during free fall the sum KE + PE stays constant - a clear illustration of conservation of energy (ignoring air resistance).

13.7 POWER

POWER is the RATE of doing work, or equivalently the rate at which energy is transferred or transformed:
   P = W / t
where W is the work done (or energy used) and t is the time taken. Power tells us how FAST work is done. Two machines may do the same work, but the one that does it in less time is more powerful.

SI unit of power: The SI unit of power is the WATT (symbol W). One watt is one joule of work done per second: 1 W = 1 J / 1 s = 1 J/s. Larger units: 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W; 1 megawatt (MW) = 1000000 W. The horsepower is an older unit: 1 hp = 746 W.

Worked example: A pump raises 200 kg of water through 10 m in 20 s (g = 10 m/s^2). Work = m g h = 200 x 10 x 10 = 20000 J. Power = W / t = 20000 / 20 = 1000 W = 1 kW.

13.8 COMMERCIAL UNIT OF ELECTRICAL ENERGY

The joule is a very small unit for measuring the large amounts of electrical energy used in homes and factories. For commercial purposes electrical energy is measured in the KILOWATT-HOUR (kWh), also called the 'unit' of electricity (Board of Trade unit). One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed when a device of power 1 kilowatt runs for 1 hour:
   1 kWh = 1 kW x 1 h = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3600000 J = 3.6 x 10^6 J
So your home electricity bill is charged per kWh, not per joule.

Worked example: A 100 W bulb runs for 10 hours. Energy = power x time = 100 W x 10 h = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh. At a tariff of (say) Rs 5 per unit, the cost is Rs 5.

SUMMARY

- Work is done only when a force acts on a body and the body is displaced: W = F s cos(theta). Work is a scalar measured in joules (1 J = 1 N m).
- Work is positive (force along motion), negative (force opposite motion) or zero (force perpendicular to motion, or zero displacement).
- Energy is the capacity to do work; it has the same unit as work, the joule.
- Kinetic energy KE = (1/2) m v^2 is the energy of motion; potential energy PE = m g h is the energy of position. The work-energy theorem says net work = change in KE.
- Energy exists in many forms - mechanical, heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical, nuclear - and can be transformed from one form to another.
- Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed; total energy is constant. In free fall, KE + PE = constant.
- Power is the rate of doing work, P = W / t, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
- The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

chapter_summary.title: Work and Energy - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 13 explains the scientific meaning of work (W = F s cos theta), defines energy as the capacity to do work, develops kinetic and potential energy, states the law of conservation of energy, and introduces power and the commercial unit of electrical energy.

sections.heading: Work in science
bullets: Work is done only when a force acts on a body AND the body is displaced; if either is zero, no work is done.
For a force F and displacement s at angle theta between them, W = F s cos(theta); when force and motion are along the same line, W = F s.
Work is positive (force along motion, cos 0 = 1), negative (force opposite, cos 180 = -1) or zero (force perpendicular, cos 90 = 0).
The SI unit of work is the joule (J): 1 J = 1 N x 1 m. Work is a scalar quantity.

sections.heading: Energy and its forms
bullets: Energy is the capacity to do work, measured by the total work a body can do; its unit is the joule, the same as work.
Forms of energy include mechanical, heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical and nuclear energy.
Energy can be transformed from one form to another, e.g. electrical to light in a bulb, chemical to electrical in a battery.

sections.heading: Kinetic and potential energy
bullets: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: KE = (1/2) m v^2; it depends on mass and the square of speed.
Gravitational potential energy is the energy of position: PE = m g h, equal to the work done against gravity to raise the body.
The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

sections.heading: Conservation of energy
bullets: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed.
The total energy of an isolated system stays constant during any transformation.
In free fall, as a body descends PE converts to KE while KE + PE stays constant; just before impact all PE has become KE.

sections.heading: Power and commercial unit
bullets: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: P = W / t; it measures how fast work is done.
The SI unit of power is the watt: 1 W = 1 J/s; larger units are the kilowatt (1000 W) and megawatt.
The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J, the energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour.

key_takeaways: Work is done only when a force displaces a body: W = F s cos(theta); the SI unit is the joule.
Work can be positive, negative or zero depending on the angle between force and displacement.
Energy is the capacity to do work and shares the joule with work; it exists in many forms that can transform into one another.
Kinetic energy KE = (1/2) m v^2 (energy of motion) and potential energy PE = m g h (energy of position) are the two forms of mechanical energy.
The law of conservation of energy holds that total energy is constant; in free fall KE + PE remains constant.
Power is the rate of doing work, P = W / t, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Work and Energy (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) Worksheet for Lesson 13. Attempt all questions. Take g = 10 m/s^2 unless stated otherwise. Show your working for numerical problems.

questions.question: Define work in the scientific sense and state the two conditions necessary for work to be done. Why does a man holding a heavy load on his head while standing still do no work?
questions.answer:
Work is said to be done when a force acts on a body and the body is displaced in the direction of (or against) the force. W = F s cos(theta).
Two conditions: (1) a force must act on the body, and (2) the body must be displaced. If either is zero, no work is done.
A man holding a load while standing still applies an upward force but the load has NO displacement (s = 0), so W = 0. He feels tired because his muscles use chemical energy to stay contracted, but in the scientific sense no work is done on the load.
questions.explanation: Definition + the two conditions + the s = 0 case.

questions.question: Distinguish between positive, negative and zero work, giving one example of each.
questions.answer:
Positive work: force (or its component) is in the direction of displacement; theta = 0, cos(0) = 1, W = F s > 0. Example: a horse pulling a cart forward.
Negative work: force is opposite to the displacement; theta = 180 degrees, cos(180) = -1, W = -F s < 0. Example: friction acting on a sliding box, or gravity on a ball moving upward.
Zero work: force is perpendicular to displacement (theta = 90 degrees, cos 90 = 0) or there is no displacement. Example: a coolie carrying a load horizontally (lift force is vertical), or the moon's centripetal force.
questions.explanation: Sign of work depends on cos(theta).

questions.question: A force of 50 N pulls a box and moves it 8 m along the direction of the force. Calculate the work done. State the unit.
questions.answer:
Given F = 50 N, s = 8 m, force along displacement so theta = 0 and cos(theta) = 1.
Work done W = F s cos(theta) = 50 x 8 x 1 = 400 J.
The work done is 400 joules (J).
questions.explanation: Direct application of W = F s.

questions.question: Define energy. State its SI unit. List any four forms of energy.
questions.answer:
Energy is the capacity (or ability) to do work. A body that can do work possesses energy, and its energy equals the total work it can do.
SI unit: the joule (J) - the same unit as work.
Four forms of energy: kinetic (mechanical) energy, heat energy, light energy, electrical energy. (Others: sound, chemical, nuclear, potential energy.)

questions.question: Derive the expression for the kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v, starting from the definition of work. State the work-energy theorem.
questions.answer:
Consider a body of mass m initially at rest (u = 0) acted on by a constant force F that accelerates it uniformly to speed v over a displacement s.
By Newton's second law, F = m a.
Using the equation of motion v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s with u = 0: v^2 = 2 a s, so a = v^2 / (2 s).
The work done by the force is W = F s = (m a) s = m [v^2 / (2 s)] s = (1/2) m v^2.
This work is stored in the body as the energy of motion, the kinetic energy:
   KE = (1/2) m v^2.
Work-energy theorem: the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, W = KE_final - KE_initial. If the body starts from rest, the work done equals the kinetic energy gained.
questions.explanation: Derivation via F = ma and v^2 = u^2 + 2as, then state the theorem.

questions.question: A 4 kg body moves with a speed of 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy. If the speed doubles, by what factor does the kinetic energy change?
questions.answer:
KE = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2)(4)(6^2) = (1/2)(4)(36) = 72 J.
Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed. If the speed doubles (v -> 2v), KE becomes (1/2) m (2v)^2 = 4 x (1/2) m v^2, i.e. 4 times the original. So the new KE = 4 x 72 = 288 J. The kinetic energy increases by a factor of 4.
questions.explanation: KE proportional to v^2; doubling v quadruples KE.

questions.question: A boy of mass 40 kg climbs a staircase of vertical height 5 m. Calculate the work done against gravity and the gain in his potential energy (g = 10 m/s^2).
questions.answer:
Work done against gravity = gain in potential energy = m g h.
Given m = 40 kg, g = 10 m/s^2, h = 5 m.
PE = m g h = 40 x 10 x 5 = 2000 J.
So the work done against gravity is 2000 J, and his potential energy increases by 2000 J.
questions.explanation: PE = m g h, equal to work done against gravity.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of energy. A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m. Using g = 10 m/s^2, find (a) its potential energy at the top, (b) its kinetic energy and speed just before hitting the ground, and (c) verify that total energy is conserved.
questions.answer:
Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.
Given m = 0.5 kg, h = 20 m, g = 10 m/s^2.
(a) At the top the ball is at rest, so KE = 0 and PE = m g h = 0.5 x 10 x 20 = 100 J. Total energy at top = 100 J.
(b) Just before hitting the ground h = 0, so PE = 0. By conservation, all PE has become KE: KE = 100 J.
From KE = (1/2) m v^2: 100 = (1/2)(0.5) v^2 = 0.25 v^2, so v^2 = 400 and v = 20 m/s.
(c) Total energy at the bottom = KE + PE = 100 + 0 = 100 J, equal to the 100 J at the top. Energy is conserved (PE was converted entirely into KE).
questions.explanation: Apply PE = m g h, conservation KE + PE = constant, then KE = (1/2) m v^2.

questions.question: Define power and state its SI unit. A machine does 6000 J of work in 30 s. Calculate its power.
questions.answer:
Power is the rate of doing work (or the rate of transferring energy): P = W / t. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
Given W = 6000 J, t = 30 s.
P = W / t = 6000 / 30 = 200 W.
The power of the machine is 200 watts.

questions.question: What is meant by the commercial unit of electrical energy? Show that 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours; find the energy used in kWh.
questions.answer:
The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), also called one 'unit' of electricity. It is the energy consumed by a device of power 1 kilowatt operating for 1 hour.
1 kWh = 1 kW x 1 h = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3 600 000 J = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
For the heater: energy = power x time = 2 kW x 3 h = 6 kWh.
So the heater uses 6 units (6 kWh) of electrical energy.
questions.explanation: Definition + unit conversion + energy = power x time.

questions.question: Power is the rate of doing work.
One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 x 10^6 joules.
The general formula for work done is W = F s ____.
questions.explanation: Only the component of force along displacement does work.

questions.question: The SI unit of work is the ____.
When force is perpendicular to displacement, the work done is ____.
A force of 5 N moving a body 4 m in its direction does ____ J of work.
Energy is defined as the capacity to do ____.
Energy stored in fuels and food is called ____ energy.
The energy possessed by a body due to its motion is ____ energy.
A 2 kg body moving at 5 m/s has kinetic energy of ____ J.
The gravitational potential energy of a body is given by the formula ____.
questions.explanation: Work done against gravity to raise the body.

questions.question: A 4 kg body raised to 5 m (g = 10) has PE of ____ J.
According to the law of conservation of energy, the total energy of an isolated system remains ____.
questions.explanation: Energy is only transformed, not created or destroyed.

questions.question: During free fall, the sum of kinetic and potential energy of a body remains ____.
Power is the rate of doing ____.
The SI unit of power is the ____.
The commercial unit of electrical energy is the ____.
State the two conditions necessary for work to be done.
questions.answer: (1) A force must act on the body, and (2) the body must be displaced (move some distance) in the direction of, or against, the force. If either the force or the displacement is zero, no work is done.

questions.question: Explain why no work is done when a person pushes hard against a rigid wall.
questions.answer: Although the person applies a large force, the wall does not move, so the displacement is zero (s = 0). Since W = F s cos(theta) and s = 0, the work done is zero. The person feels tired because muscles consume chemical energy, but in the scientific sense no work is done on the wall.

questions.question: A force of 25 N displaces a body 6 m in the direction of the force. Find the work done.
questions.answer: Force and displacement are along the same line, so theta = 0 and cos(theta) = 1. W = F s cos(theta) = 25 x 6 x 1 = 150 J. The work done is 150 joules.

questions.question: A force of 60 N is applied at an angle of 60 degrees to the horizontal, moving a box 5 m horizontally. Calculate the work done (cos 60 = 0.5).
questions.answer: Only the horizontal component of the force does work on the horizontally-moving box. W = F s cos(theta) = 60 x 5 x cos(60) = 60 x 5 x 0.5 = 150 J. The work done is 150 joules.

questions.question: Give one example each of positive work and negative work.
questions.answer: Positive work: a person pushing a trolley forward - force and displacement are in the same direction (W = +F s). Negative work: friction acting on a sliding object - the friction force opposes the displacement, so it does negative work (W = -F s).
questions.explanation: Sign depends on direction of force vs motion.

questions.question: Define one joule of work.
questions.answer: One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves a body through a distance of 1 metre in the direction of the force. 1 J = 1 N x 1 m = 1 N m.

questions.question: What is energy? Name its SI unit.
questions.answer: Energy is the capacity (ability) to do work. A body that can do work possesses energy. Its SI unit is the joule (J), the same as the unit of work.

questions.question: List six different forms of energy.
questions.answer: Six forms of energy: (1) mechanical energy (kinetic + potential), (2) heat (thermal) energy, (3) light energy, (4) sound energy, (5) electrical energy, (6) chemical energy. (A seventh is nuclear energy, stored in the atomic nucleus.)

questions.question: Describe the energy transformations that take place in a hydroelectric power station.
questions.answer: Water is stored at a height behind a dam, so it has gravitational potential energy. When the water falls, this potential energy is converted into kinetic energy of the moving water. The fast-moving water turns turbines, converting kinetic energy into mechanical energy, and the turbines drive generators that convert mechanical energy into electrical energy. The total energy is conserved throughout.

questions.question: State the energy conversions in (a) an electric bulb and (b) an electric fan.
questions.answer: (a) In an electric bulb, electrical energy is converted into light energy and heat energy. (b) In an electric fan, electrical energy is converted into mechanical (kinetic) energy of the rotating blades, with some heat and sound also produced.

questions.question: Define kinetic energy and write its formula.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body because of its motion. For a body of mass m moving with speed v, KE = (1/2) m v^2. It is measured in joules and is always positive.

questions.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 3 kg body moving at 4 m/s.
questions.answer: KE = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2)(3)(4^2) = (1/2)(3)(16) = 24 J. The kinetic energy is 24 joules.

questions.question: A 1500 kg car increases its speed from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. Find the work done by the engine.
questions.answer: By the work-energy theorem, work done = change in kinetic energy. Initial KE = (1/2)(1500)(10^2) = 750 x 100 = 75000 J. Final KE = (1/2)(1500)(20^2) = 750 x 400 = 300000 J. Work done = 300000 - 75000 = 225000 J = 225 kJ.

questions.question: State the work-energy theorem.
questions.answer: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body is equal to the change in its kinetic energy: W = KE_final - KE_initial. If the body starts from rest, the work done equals the kinetic energy it gains.

questions.question: How does the kinetic energy of a body change if (a) its mass is doubled, (b) its speed is doubled? Explain.
questions.answer: KE = (1/2) m v^2. (a) If mass is doubled (m -> 2m) at the same speed, KE becomes (1/2)(2m) v^2 = 2 x [(1/2) m v^2], i.e. it doubles. (b) If speed is doubled (v -> 2v), KE becomes (1/2) m (2v)^2 = 4 x [(1/2) m v^2], i.e. it becomes four times, because KE depends on the square of the speed.
questions.explanation: KE proportional to m and to v^2.

questions.question: A body of mass 2 kg has kinetic energy 36 J. Find its speed.
questions.answer: KE = (1/2) m v^2, so 36 = (1/2)(2) v^2 = v^2. Therefore v^2 = 36 and v = 6 m/s. The speed of the body is 6 m/s.

questions.question: Define potential energy and give the formula for gravitational potential energy.
questions.answer: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its position or configuration. Gravitational potential energy, due to a body's height h above the ground, is PE = m g h, where m is mass and g is the acceleration due to gravity.

questions.question: Calculate the potential energy of a 6 kg body raised to a height of 3 m (g = 10 m/s^2).
questions.answer: PE = m g h = 6 x 10 x 3 = 180 J. The potential energy is 180 joules.

questions.question: A 2 kg book is lifted from the floor onto a shelf 1.5 m high (g = 10 m/s^2). Find the work done against gravity and the gain in potential energy.
questions.answer: Work done against gravity equals the gain in potential energy. PE = m g h = 2 x 10 x 1.5 = 30 J. So the work done against gravity is 30 J and the book gains 30 J of potential energy.

questions.question: Why does a body lifted to a greater height possess more potential energy?
questions.answer: Gravitational potential energy is PE = m g h, which is directly proportional to the height h. To raise a body to a greater height, more work must be done against gravity, and this extra work is stored as additional potential energy. Hence a greater height means greater potential energy (for the same mass).

questions.question: A crane lifts a 500 kg load to a height of 12 m (g = 10 m/s^2). Find the potential energy gained. If it then drops, what will its kinetic energy be just before reaching the ground?
questions.answer: PE gained = m g h = 500 x 10 x 12 = 60000 J = 60 kJ. By conservation of energy, if the load falls freely from that height, all the potential energy converts to kinetic energy, so just before reaching the ground KE = 60000 J = 60 kJ (ignoring air resistance).
questions.explanation: PE = m g h; conservation gives KE = PE.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

questions.question: For a body in free fall, explain how kinetic and potential energy change, and what stays constant.
questions.answer: At the top, the body is at rest: KE = 0 and PE = m g H (maximum). As it falls, height decreases so PE decreases, while speed increases so KE increases. At every instant the sum KE + PE remains constant and equal to m g H. Just before hitting the ground, PE = 0 and all the energy is kinetic: (1/2) m v^2 = m g H. This illustrates conservation of mechanical energy (ignoring air resistance).
questions.explanation: PE -> KE while KE + PE = constant.

questions.question: A 2 kg stone is dropped from a height of 10 m (g = 10 m/s^2). Find its potential energy at the top and its speed just before hitting the ground.
questions.answer: PE at top = m g h = 2 x 10 x 10 = 200 J. By conservation, just before hitting the ground all of it becomes kinetic energy: KE = 200 J. Then 200 = (1/2)(2) v^2 = v^2, so v^2 = 200 and v = sqrt(200) = about 14.1 m/s (or using v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(200)).
questions.explanation: Conservation: PE at top = KE at bottom.

questions.question: A pendulum bob swings back and forth. Describe the energy changes during one swing (assume no friction).
questions.answer: At the highest point of the swing the bob is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic energy is zero and its potential energy is maximum. As it swings down, potential energy converts into kinetic energy, so KE increases and PE decreases. At the lowest point KE is maximum and PE is minimum. As it rises on the other side, KE converts back into PE. Throughout the swing the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant, since there is no friction.
questions.explanation: KE and PE interchange; total constant.

questions.question: Define power and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Power is the rate of doing work, or the rate at which energy is transferred: P = W / t, where W is the work done and t is the time taken. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.

questions.question: A worker does 1200 J of work in 4 minutes. Calculate the average power.
questions.answer: Time t = 4 minutes = 4 x 60 = 240 s. Power P = W / t = 1200 / 240 = 5 W. The average power is 5 watts.
questions.explanation: Convert time to seconds, then P = W/t.

questions.question: An electric motor lifts 150 kg of water through 8 m in 10 s (g = 10 m/s^2). Find the power of the motor.
questions.answer: Work done = m g h = 150 x 10 x 8 = 12000 J. Power P = W / t = 12000 / 10 = 1200 W = 1.2 kW. The power of the motor is 1200 watts.

questions.question: A house uses a 1.5 kW geyser for 2 hours daily. Find the energy consumed per day in kWh and in joules.
questions.answer: Energy per day = power x time = 1.5 kW x 2 h = 3 kWh. In joules: 3 kWh x 3.6 x 10^6 J/kWh = 10.8 x 10^6 J = 1.08 x 10^7 J. So the geyser uses 3 units (3 kWh = 1.08 x 10^7 J) per day.
questions.explanation: Energy = P x t; convert kWh to J.

questions.question: Why is the kilowatt-hour used instead of the joule for measuring household electrical energy?
questions.answer: The joule is a very small unit, so the electrical energy used in homes would be expressed as enormous numbers of joules (millions or more). The kilowatt-hour is much larger (1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J), giving convenient, manageable numbers for billing. Hence electricity bills are charged per kWh ('unit').

questions.question: Ravi pushes a loaded cart of total mass 50 kg along a level road. He applies a horizontal force of 120 N and the cart moves 10 m in the direction of the force. A frictional force of 40 N opposes the motion. (a) What is the work done by Ravi? (b) What is the work done by friction? (c) What is the net work done on the cart? (d) Name the type of work done by friction.
questions.answer:
(a) Work by Ravi: force is along displacement, so W = F s = 120 x 10 = 1200 J (positive).
(b) Work by friction: friction opposes motion (theta = 180), W = -40 x 10 = -400 J (negative).
(c) Net work = 1200 + (-400) = 800 J. (Equivalently, net force = 120 - 40 = 80 N, so W = 80 x 10 = 800 J.)
(d) Friction does NEGATIVE work because it acts opposite to the displacement.
questions.explanation: Positive, negative and net work on the cart.

questions.question: A porter at a railway station lifts a 20 kg suitcase from the platform to a height of 1.5 m and places it on his head. He then walks 50 m along the level platform carrying the suitcase, and finally stands still for 2 minutes (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the work done in lifting the suitcase. (b) How much work is done while walking the 50 m horizontally? (c) How much work is done while standing still? (d) Explain your answer to part (b).
questions.answer:
(a) Work in lifting = m g h = 20 x 10 x 1.5 = 300 J (work done against gravity).
(b) Work while walking horizontally = 0 J. The lifting force (supporting the suitcase) is vertical while the displacement is horizontal, so the angle between them is 90 degrees and cos(90) = 0.
(c) Work while standing still = 0 J, because there is no displacement (s = 0).
(d) During horizontal walking the upward supporting force is perpendicular to the horizontal motion, so it does no work (W = F s cos 90 = 0), even though the porter feels he is working.
questions.explanation: Zero work when force is perpendicular to motion.

questions.question: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg is bowled at a speed of 30 m/s. A batsman hits it back so that it leaves the bat at 40 m/s in the opposite direction. (a) Find the kinetic energy of the ball before being hit. (b) Find its kinetic energy after being hit. (c) By how much did the kinetic energy change? (d) What supplied this energy change?
questions.answer:
(a) KE before = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2)(0.16)(30^2) = 0.08 x 900 = 72 J.
(b) KE after = (1/2)(0.16)(40^2) = 0.08 x 1600 = 128 J.
(c) Change in KE = 128 - 72 = 56 J (an increase).
(d) The work done by the batsman (the force of the bat) supplied this 56 J increase in kinetic energy, in accordance with the work-energy theorem.

questions.question: A truck of mass 2000 kg and a car of mass 1000 kg are both moving at the same speed of 15 m/s on a highway. (a) Find the kinetic energy of the truck. (b) Find the kinetic energy of the car. (c) Which vehicle has greater kinetic energy and why? (d) If both are brought to rest, which needs more braking work?
questions.answer:
(a) KE of truck = (1/2)(2000)(15^2) = 1000 x 225 = 225000 J = 225 kJ.
(b) KE of car = (1/2)(1000)(15^2) = 500 x 225 = 112500 J = 112.5 kJ.
(c) The truck has greater kinetic energy because, at the same speed, KE is proportional to mass and the truck has twice the mass of the car.
(d) The truck needs more braking work - the braking work must remove all the kinetic energy, and the truck has more KE (225 kJ vs 112.5 kJ).
questions.explanation: KE proportional to mass at fixed speed.

questions.question: Water is stored in an overhead tank of capacity holding 1000 kg of water at a height of 8 m above the ground (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the potential energy of the stored water. (b) If the water falls to the ground, what is its kinetic energy just before reaching the ground? (c) Find the speed of the water just before impact. (d) Which law did you use in part (b)?
questions.answer:
(a) PE = m g h = 1000 x 10 x 8 = 80000 J = 80 kJ.
(b) By conservation of energy, all the potential energy becomes kinetic energy: KE = 80000 J = 80 kJ (ignoring losses).
(c) From KE = (1/2) m v^2: 80000 = (1/2)(1000) v^2 = 500 v^2, so v^2 = 160 and v = sqrt(160) = about 12.6 m/s. (Or v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(160).)
(d) The law of conservation of energy.

questions.question: A ball of mass 1 kg is dropped from a height of 45 m (g = 10 m/s^2). Consider three points: the top (A), the midpoint at 22.5 m (B), and just above the ground (C). (a) Find the total mechanical energy at A. (b) Find the PE and KE at B. (c) Find the KE and speed at C. (d) What stays constant throughout?
questions.answer:
(a) At A: KE = 0, PE = m g h = 1 x 10 x 45 = 450 J. Total mechanical energy = 450 J.
(b) At B (h = 22.5 m): PE = 1 x 10 x 22.5 = 225 J. By conservation, KE = 450 - 225 = 225 J (half and half).
(c) At C (h = 0): PE = 0, so KE = 450 J. Then 450 = (1/2)(1) v^2, so v^2 = 900 and v = 30 m/s.
(d) The total mechanical energy (KE + PE = 450 J) stays constant throughout the fall, illustrating conservation of energy.
questions.explanation: KE + PE constant during free fall.

questions.question: A child on a swing is pushed once and then left to swing freely (assume negligible friction). The swing rises to a highest point on each side and moves fastest at the bottom. (a) Where is the potential energy maximum? (b) Where is the kinetic energy maximum? (c) What happens to the total energy during the swing? (d) Why does a real swing eventually stop?
questions.answer:
(a) The potential energy is maximum at the highest points of the swing (greatest height, momentarily at rest).
(b) The kinetic energy is maximum at the lowest point of the swing (greatest speed, least height).
(c) Ignoring friction, the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) stays constant; energy simply changes between PE and KE.
(d) A real swing eventually stops because friction at the pivot and air resistance gradually convert the mechanical energy into heat and sound, so the mechanical energy decreases over time.
questions.explanation: PE and KE interchange; friction dissipates energy.

questions.question: Two students climb the same staircase of vertical height 4 m. Student A has mass 50 kg and takes 8 s; student B has mass 60 kg and takes 12 s (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the work done by A against gravity. (b) Find the work done by B against gravity. (c) Find the power of each. (d) Who is more powerful?
questions.answer:
(a) Work by A = m g h = 50 x 10 x 4 = 2000 J.
(b) Work by B = 60 x 10 x 4 = 2400 J.
(c) Power of A = W / t = 2000 / 8 = 250 W. Power of B = 2400 / 12 = 200 W.
(d) Student A is more powerful (250 W > 200 W), because although A does slightly less work, A does it in less time, so the rate of doing work is greater.

questions.question: A family uses the following appliances daily: four 100 W bulbs for 5 hours each, a 1000 W refrigerator running effectively for 8 hours, and a 2000 W air conditioner for 3 hours. The electricity tariff is Rs 6 per unit (per kWh). (a) Find the daily energy used by the bulbs in kWh. (b) Find the daily energy used by the refrigerator and the AC. (c) Find the total daily energy in kWh. (d) Find the daily electricity cost.
questions.answer:
(a) Bulbs: 4 x 100 W = 400 W = 0.4 kW, for 5 h => 0.4 x 5 = 2 kWh.
(b) Refrigerator: 1000 W = 1 kW x 8 h = 8 kWh. AC: 2000 W = 2 kW x 3 h = 6 kWh.
(c) Total = 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 kWh per day.
(d) Cost = 16 units x Rs 6 = Rs 96 per day.
questions.explanation: Energy = power x time in kWh; cost = units x tariff.

questions.question: An electric pump rated 2 kW is used to lift water to a tank. In one hour it lifts 36000 kg of water to a height of 15 m (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the useful work done in lifting the water. (b) Find the electrical energy consumed in one hour in joules and in kWh. (c) Find the efficiency of the pump. (d) Why is the efficiency less than 100%?
questions.answer:
(a) Useful work = m g h = 36000 x 10 x 15 = 5400000 J = 5.4 x 10^6 J.
(b) Electrical energy = power x time = 2000 W x 3600 s = 7.2 x 10^6 J = 2 kWh.
(c) Efficiency = useful output / energy input = 5.4 x 10^6 / 7.2 x 10^6 = 0.75 = 75%.
(d) Efficiency is less than 100% because some input energy is lost as heat (in the motor and due to friction) and as sound, so not all the electrical energy goes into lifting water.
questions.explanation: Useful work vs input energy; efficiency.
